detail.title: Performance of Value Functions with Probability Weighting Functions in Prospect Theory: Evidence from Japan
detail.abstract: This paper compares the performance of alternative value functions and probability weighting functions in Prospect Theory (PT) and Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT) using experimental data from Japan. We examine power and exponential value functions combined with three commonly used weighting functions under questionnaires that differ in the number of large-stake lotteries. Model parameters are estimated using a grid-search procedure, and model performance is evaluated based on normalized errors at the individual level. The results show that the presence of multiple large-stake lotteries significantly affects model selection. Power value functions perform better when questionnaires include several large-stake lotteries, whereas exponential value functions are favored when large-stake lotteries are absent or limited to one. These findings highlight the importance of questionnaire design in empirical tests of prospect theory.

title: Geomechanical Analysis of Hot Fluid Injection in Thermal Enhanced Oil Recovery
affiliations: University of Houston

detail.title: Geomechanical Analysis of Hot Fluid Injection in Thermal Enhanced Oil Recovery
detail.abstract: Hot-fluid injection in thermal enhanced oil recovery (thermal EOR, TEOR) imposes temperature-driven volumetric strains that can substantially alter in-situ stresses, fracture geometry, and wellbore/reservoir integrity, yet existing TEOR modeling has not fully captured coupled thermo-poroelastic (thermo-hydro-mechanical) effects on fracture aperture, fracture-tip behavior, and stress rotation within a displacement discontinuity method (DDM) framework. This study aims to examine the influence of sustained hot-fluid injection on stress redistribution, hydraulic fracture deformation, and fracture stability in thermal EOR by accounting for coupled thermal, hydraulic, and mechanical interactions. This study develops a fully coupled thermo-poroelastic DDM formulation in which fracture-surface normal and shear displacement discontinuities, together with fluid and heat influx, act as boundary sources to compute time-dependent stresses, pore pressure, and temperature, while internal fracture fluid flow (Poiseuille-based volume balance), heat transport (conduction–advection with rock exchange), and mixed-mode propagation criteria are included. A representative scenario considers an initially isothermal hydraulic fracture grown to 32 m, followed by 12 months of hot-fluid injection with temperature contrasts of ΔT = 0-100 °C and reduced pumping rate. Results show that hydraulic fracture aperture increases under isothermal and modest heating (ΔT = 25 °C) and remains nearly stable near ΔT = 50 °C, but progressively narrows for ΔT = 75-100 °C despite continued injection, indicating potential injectivity decline driven by thermally induced compressive stresses. Hot injection also tightens fracture tips, restricting unintended propagation, and produces pronounced near-fracture stress amplification and re-orientation: minimum principal stress increases by 6 MPa for ΔT = 50 °C and 10 MPa for ΔT = 100 °C, with principal-stress rotation reaching 70–90° in regions adjacent to the fracture plane and markedly elevated shear stresses that may promote natural-fracture activation. These findings show that temperature effects can directly influence injectivity, fracture containment, and the risk of unintended fracture or natural-fracture activation, underscoring the importance of temperature-aware geomechanical planning and injection-strategy design in field operations. Incorporating these effects into project design can help operators anticipate injectivity decline, improve fracture containment, and reduce geomechanical uncertainty during long-term hot-fluid injection.

detail.abstract: We collect new data to document the long-run evolution of the firm size distribution in ten marketbased economies in Asia, Europe, North America, and Oceania, where we can obtain comprehensive coverage of the population of firms. Around the world, we observe prevalent increases in the concentration of sales, net income, and equity capital over the past century. These trends hold in the aggregate and at the industry level. Meanwhile, employment concentration has been stable over the long run in most cases. The evidence shows that the rising dominance of large firms is a pervasive phenomenon, not limited to the recent decades or the United States, and that large firms often achieve greater scale without proportionally more workers.

affiliations: Columbia University - Law School

detail.title: The Unitary Executive and the Federal Reserve

publicationDetails.detailsText: Columbia Public Law Research Paper Forthcoming

detail.abstract: The Supreme Court may soon embrace an interpretation of the Constitution that would significantly expand the power of the President over federal administrators and invalidate key provisions in dozens of federal statutes. A critical question is whether this interpretation—known as Unitary Executive Theory (UET)—would also render unconstitutional Central Bank Independence (CBI), an arrangement where a country’s monetary policy is formulated by a semi-autonomous body of experts insulated from partisan political pressure. Several justices have suggested that it would not, and a growing scholarly literature has proposed ways for the Court to distinguish the country’s central banking apparatus from the rest of the administrative state. This Article examines these proposals and concludes that none are tenable. It then explains why UET is fundamentally inconsistent with CBI: the Federal Reserve’s independence from the President reflects a wholly different, and incompatible, approach to the separation of powers. It further suggests that since the regulation of money and banking is one of the most important functions of the modern state, this conflict is arguably sufficient, standing alone, to reject UET. Relatedly, if the Court wishes to preserve statutory limits on the President’s power to remove Federal Reserve officials without repudiating UET outright, it has only one viable option: stare decisis.

detail.title: Rational Disagreement

detail.abstract: We propose rational disagreement as a formal framework for analyzing seemingly irrational behavior that can persist despite the wide availability of objective information in a steady-state. Agents are rational in that they correctly anticipate the distribution of aggregate outcomes, yet disagree about which specific individuals perform better than others. Notably, the subjective belief of any individual may be objectively correct. We illustrate the key concepts with a simple entry game. We show how unordered individual outcome distributions can be identified solely from aggregate statistics. We then characterize the resulting game, define its Nash equilibria, and develop a statistical test for the null hypothesis of agreement. Finally, we situate our framework within the broader literature on Bayesian games, behavioral biases, and the rational expectations hypothesis.

detail.abstract: American disability law purports to operate on principles of equality, yet it consistently distinguishes between worthy and unworthy disabled individuals based on how, when, and under what circumstances a person acquired their disability, as well as severity and type of disability. This Article examines veteran disability hierarchies as a case study in intragroup status differentiation-the ways in which members of the same identity group are valued and treated unequally in society and under the law. We analyze two primary domains: the Department of Veterans Affairs' service-connected disability compensation system and the criminal legal system's use of veterans' treatment courts and sentencing mitigation. In both contexts, formal legal structures and informal implementation practices combine to privilege certain veterans-typically male veterans with honorable discharges whose combat-related conditions fit into the cultural narrative of the warrior-hero-while excluding others with identical disabilities. Race, gender, sexual orientation, discharge status, and the circumstances of disability acquisition determine which veterans receive compassion and resources and which do not. Meanwhile, civilians with the same disabilities-PTSD from community violence or childhood trauma, traumatic brain injury from domestic abuse, substance use disorders rooted in structural deprivation-receive no such solicitude. The underlying conditions are indistinguishable; only the state's willingness to accommodate them differs. The criminal legal system's capacity for treatment-focused responses when the disabled individual is deemed a deserving veteran proves that harsh punishment of other disabled individuals is a policy choice, not a necessity. Disability Justice demands extending such compassionate responses and supports universally, rather than rationing them according to whose suffering aligns with preferred stories about heroism and sacrifice.

title: Whose Preference Counts? Intra-household Bargaining, Spousal Discordance, and the Limits of Female Agency in Indian Fertility Decisions

detail.title: Whose Preference Counts? Intra-household Bargaining, Spousal Discordance, and the Limits of Female Agency in Indian Fertility Decisions
detail.abstract: Despite India achieving replacement-level fertility, a significant "intention-action gap" persists: millions of married women explicitly state a desire to stop childbearing yet do not utilize modern contraception. This paper investigates the demandside drivers of this paradox by testing the "Husband's Veto" hypothesis within a noncooperative bargaining framework. Using dyadic data from the National Family to dismantle structural authority. Our results imply that family planning policies must pivot from "demand generation" to "barrier removal," prioritizing male engagement and contraceptive technologies that minimize negotiation costs-particularly in high-veto regions. These findings highlight the limits of individual empowerment in the face of entrenched patriarchal norms, with implications for other settings where kinship regimes constrain women's reproductive autonomy.

title: From Representation to Deployment Why Fiscal Geometry requires a Specification Layer

detail.title: From Representation to Deployment Why Fiscal Geometry requires a Specification Layer
detail.abstract:
Fiscal Geometry (FG) has been developed in prior working papers as a representational
discipline: a formal X–Y grammar that renders institutional rule-systems as inspectable
structures (events, routes, gates, and visibility constraints) and compares change through S₀/S₁/Δ
differences. Yet the existence of a coherent theory and multiple domain specimens does not, by
itself, make FG deployable in professional workflows. A practical gap remains between
“readable papers” and “usable artifacts”: institutions adopt forms that can be executed, audited,
handed over, and reproduced under time pressure and responsibility.
This bridging note introduces a specification layer for FG—a general blueprint that converts the
method into a workflow object. The specification fixes (i) input boundaries (artifact corridors
and observation windows), (ii) minimal construction artifacts (Edges and Anchors tables, plus
R/G/V mapping), (iii) standardized outputs (S₀/S₁ assembly and Δ reporting), and (iv) basic
validation hooks for reproducibility and auditability. The aim is not to add new theory, but to
change FG’s operational status: from a representational argument to an executable form.
To demonstrate applicability without collapsing into case-writing, the note sketches three
minimal “test fields” in which the same blueprint can be instantiated: assurance/audit working-
paper addenda, cross-border capital-market gate mapping, and an AI-era structural audit layer
that makes institutional outputs reviewable before responsibility is assigned. The result is a
compact entry point for adoption: FG as a deployable specification rather than a growing list of
papers.
This note introduces an executable specification layer for Fiscal Geometry; readers seeking the
theoretical foundations are referred to the author’s prior working papers—Fiscal Geometry as a
Methodological Meta-Grammar for Institutional Analysis (Abstract ID 5994694), Information
Before Action: A Fiscal-Epistemic Framework for Institutional and Interdisciplinary Analysis
(Abstract ID 6014054), and FG Protocol & Reproducibility Notes—which establish FG’s
representational grammar and methodological basis

detail.abstract: This study analyzes how financial indicators influence credit ratings by utilizing corporate data from domestic credit rating agency. Among 24 financial indicators, significant indicators and their relative impacts were estimated using the System Generalized Method of Moments. The indicators were categorized into five credit rating evaluation factors: profitability, stability, liquidity, activity, and growth. It was found that at least one indicator from each of the five factors significantly influenced credit ratings. The key indicators include the cash asset ratio (liquidity), the equity ratio (stability), the total asset turnover (activity), the equity growth rate (growth), and the interest coverage ratio (profitability). Sensitivity to credit ratings was particularly high for the liquidity and stability indicators, indicating differences in the relative impact of each indicator. These findings suggest that the selected indicators are well-distributed across the factors, and the varying influence of the selected variables can provide valuable insights for informing companies on which indicators to focus on when managing their credit ratings. Additionally, it can verify the appropriateness of the weighting of evaluation factors used by credit rating agency.

title: Investors’ Trading on Past Returns and their Trading Impact on Stock Returns
affiliations: , Ming Chuan University, University of Houston and Shu-Te University

detail.title: Investors’ Trading on Past Returns and their Trading Impact on Stock Returns
detail.abstract: This paper extends the return-volume literature by examining the dynamic, bidirectional implications of seven largely unexplored trading theories: analyst optimism, social interaction, style trading, investor disagreement, and investor attention (both firm-specific and marketspecific for the latter two). Following Chordia et al. (2011), we use firm-level data to capture heterogeneity that market-index data may obscure. Our main findings are as follows. First, return-volume relations exhibit substantial heterogeneity in both directions. Second, investors trade more actively following high returns at the stock, style, and market levels and respond more aggressively to positive returns than to negative ones. Third, investor sentiment amplifies these patterns: trading on past high returns is more frequent during high-sentiment periods. Finally, we introduce a novel decomposition of trading volume into three past return-driven components, which exert upward price pressure on the traded stocks. Stocks subject to greater pressure tend to be overpriced. These results provide empirical support for the theories of analyst optimism, style trading, firm-specific disagreement, and firm-specific attention.

detail.abstract: The study analyzes the impact of financial digitalization on the asset soundness and bank-run risk of savings banks. This study empirically examines how digitalization, particularly the expansion of mobile applications, affects asset soundness and bank-run risk in Korean savings banks. In recent years, savings bank have increasingly adopted mobile banking apps to attract customers and expand their non-face-to-face services. However, due to the characteristics of saving banks, which are heavily reliant on lending to medium- to low-credit borrowers and deposits, digitalization can led to a higher influx of vulnerable borrowers and potential asset deterioration. Furthermore, the ease of mobile-based withdrawals may amplify bank run risks during external crises. This research empirically examines the effects of digitalization on asset soundness and liquidity risks in savings banks, demonstrating that digital transformation can be a critical factor in risk management for financial institutions. Through this analysis, the study highlights the importance of stricter risk management strategies as financial institutions face the challenges posed by digital services expansion.

detail.title: Two-Stage Volatility-Quantile Models using Deep Learning Density Networks with Application to Cryptocurrencies
detail.abstract: Recently, deep learning density networks have become the standard baselines for financial timeseries forecasting. In this paper, we introduce density networks structured using the two-stage volatility to return models, in which the volatility forecast are treated as an input to the scale parameter of the second stage return model. The models employ a negative log-likelihood loss for both stages, which is constructed from the Weibull or a generalized beta distribution for stage one and normal (Gaussian) or Student-t for stage two. VaR is computed directly from the fitted returns distribution using mean regression. However, it is well known that effects on the mean can differ substantially to those on the extreme quantiles, the focus for risk management in investment portfolios. Hence, nonparametric quantile and expectile regressions are considered by extending the return loss to asymmetric Laplace and Gaussian proxy distributions. The time varying variance from first stage weights the observations inversely to their variances. Our empirical examination focuses on daily returns and Parkinson volatility measures of Bitcoin and Ripple. In comparing with the parametric VaR, the nonparametric quantiles and expectiles shows great adaptiveness and accuracy to observed data.

detail.abstract: The SVB resolution in the US and the merger of Credit Suisse in Switzerland have raised the need for a special resolution regime. The current resolution regime is based on the assumption of insolvency, which means that intervention for resolution purposes is not allowed unless net worth is negative, and the process is complicated. However, waiting for the net worth of a crisis financial institution to become negative may increase systemic risk in the market. Therefore, it is necessary to consider a special resolution regime that provides for early intervention and rapid resolution, which is different from the normal resolution process. D-SIFIs should be the first to be considered for a special resolution regime. Special requirements are needed to ensure that a financial firm's net worth is not negative and that intervention for resolution purposes is possible. Special requirements are defined as a financial institution that is unlikely to be able to recover on its own without a special loan from the central bank or funding from public funds, and is likely to pose a systemic risk. To make this determination, a provisional valuation is required, which requires an independent assessor and evaluation criteria. The decision on whether to initiate a special resolution process based on the results of the provisional valuation should be made by a separate committee composed of members of the FSC and external experts. The results of the valuation should be verified by formal valuation at a later date. In the case of a liquidation despite a positive net worth, the issue of infringement of property rights of shareholders is raised. Therefore, at a minimum, shareholders should be guaranteed the liquidation value in accordance with the NCWOL principle, and if the value is not guaranteed, compensation should be paid to the extent of the guaranteed liquidation value, because infringement of property rights may constitute expropriation. The initiation of a special resolution regime can be contested by way of an appeal. In addition, if there has been a violation in the initiation of the proceedings and the process, state compensation may be claimed. Therefore, in order to reduce the likelihood of litigation, it is important to comply with the procedures and ensure the independence of the provisional valuation.

detail.title: ECBetas in Equity Strategy Returns
detail.abstract: Using high-frequency overnight index swap (OIS) surprises around ECB Governing Council meetings, we uncover a sharp monetary policy risk-return tradeoff in a cross-section of 153 long-short equity factors. Equity strategies more exposed to ECB monetary policy shocks – those with lower OIS betas – earn higher excess returns and Sharpe ratios. Results strengthen using asset pricing methods that account for measurement errors and omitted variables. This risk premium arises primarily in the press release window – i.e. the monetary policy decision – and displays a tent-shaped pattern that peaks with OIS surprises between six-month and two-year tenors.

detail.abstract:
Objective. We test whether high research and development (R&D) intensity predicts higher subsequent equity returns in a large-cap U.S. universe using methodology designed for portfolio implementability.

Method. Each year, we sort an S&P 500 large-cap universe into quintiles by R&D intensity (R&D expense divided by revenue) and evaluate subsequent July-June returns to mitigate look-ahead bias. The annual high-minus-low premium series (HML_RD, Q5-Q1) spans Jul1995–Jun1996 to Jul2024–Jun2025 (30 observations). Primary statistical inference uses monthly Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions (360 months) and monthly factor spanning tests, which provide sufficient power to detect the premium.

Results. The high-minus-low R&D factor (HML_RD) averages 3.73% per year (t = 1.10, p = 0.2793; Newey-West), positive in 17/30 years (57% win rate). At monthly frequency, factor spanning tests confirm a statistically distinct premium (FF5 α = 4.37%, p < 0.01). Monthly Fama-MacBeth regressions provide directionally consistent cross-sectional evidence after controlling for size and book-to-market (p = 0.0737). The investable RD20 strategy delivers 7.52% annual excess return versus SPY after transaction costs (Jul2001–Jun2025 backtest, N=24), retaining 99.6% of the gross premium.

Implementation. We map the signal into a simple long-only portfolio that holds the top 20 stocks by R&D intensity (equal-weighted) and reconstitutes annually in July.

Interpretation. Results are consistent with either mispricing of intangible assets or risk compensation for innovation exposure. We document sector tilts, factor exposures, and regime dependence without claiming to isolate a single mechanism. The analysis is associational rather than causal.

detail.abstract:
Transportation law has a congestion problem: our federalist system of government allows federal and state actors to stymie innovative, locally driven projects that aim to reduce driving. This problem is illustrated in the decades-long legal battles over New York City’s plan to impose “congestion pricing” to toll drivers entering certain parts of Manhattan. Overcoming grandstanding elected officials, lawsuits resting on state and federal supremacy, and even a federal legislative override, congestion pricing was finally launched in January 2025. New Yorkers and suburbanites alike almost immediately started benefiting from cleaner air, faster commutes, safer roads, and increased economic activity and productivity—plus boatloads of money for transit improvements. Just six weeks later, however, the Trump administration Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy announced he was unilaterally rescinding federal approval for the program, once again throwing it into legal limbo.

Through the lens of congestion pricing and its unique characteristics, this Essay illustrates the relatively limited power of local and regional authorities to advance innovative transportation initiatives through the federal and state permitting gauntlet. Part I relates the congestion-pricing backstory in New York City from its origins in the late nineteenth century, to federal and state officials’ unwelcome intervention at key points, to its approval last year. Part II covers the latest attempt to roll back congestion pricing and the pending case of Metropolitan Transportation Authority v. Duffy, a federal lawsuit filed against Secretary Duffy by the regional body that operates the New York City congestion pricing program. Part III argues that new legal approaches that safeguard local interests are necessary. It identifies several judicial and congressional measures that may afford local governments more latitude to plan and carry out their transportation priorities and that may offer innovative, decarbonizing projects a higher priority in permitting.

title: Credit Allocation under Physical and Transition Climate Risks

detail.abstract: This paper studies how banks adjust credit allocation in response to firms' exposure to climate-related physical and transition risks, with a focus on non-listed SMEs. Using granular firm-level measures of both risk types matched to a universal bankfirm credit dataset from Danish administrative registers, I document that banks reduce credit growth to firms with higher exposure to either risk. A one standard deviation increase in physical (transition) risk is associated with a 1.1-1.4% (1.6-2.2%) decline in loan growth. Beyond average effects, I find evidence of credit reallocation across firms with heterogeneous risk profiles: more credit is allocated to firms with low joint exposure to physical and transition risks and to high-risk firms that engage in greening activities. Credit contractions are strongest when climate risks compound existing borrower vulnerabilities, such as financial constraints and asset exposure, and among banks with higher climate risk exposure and repeat lending relationships. Mechanism tests indicate that banks' credit risk considerations play an important role in driving these credit responses.

title: Memory Shapes Reaction to Extreme Returns in Stock Sale Decisions
affiliations: University of Warwick - Department of Statistics,  and University of Warwick

detail.title: Memory Shapes Reaction to Extreme Returns in Stock Sale Decisions
detail.abstract: We provide empirical evidence on how selective memory shapes the propensity for an investor to realize the sale of stocks in their portfolio after observing extreme stock and market returns. It is well known that investors are more likely to sell stocks that had a large return on the previous day. We observe that investor reactions to such extreme events, or cues, are significantly affected by their own past realized returns. Investors whose best past realized returns were higher, tend to react less to an extreme positive stock or market return. Those with lower worst past realized returns tend to react more to extreme negative stock or market returns. The impact of the memories of the worst realized returns on the propensity to sell is greater, the more recently those worst returns were experienced. We also find that memory effects are stronger for more attentive and sophisticated investors. Our empirical findings are consistent with the principles of selective memory, a process of memory retrieval guided by similarity, which influences belief formation. Our results also demonstrate a positive memory bias.

title: From Product to Infrastructure Reframing Physical Environments in Early Childhood Institutions

detail.title: From Product to Infrastructure Reframing Physical Environments in Early Childhood Institutions
detail.abstract: This paper argues that certain physical environments used in early childhood institutions are systematically misclassified as discretionary products rather than institutional infrastructure. This classification error is not semantic. It shapes how such environments are designed, procured, governed, and maintained. And, it materially affects how responsibility for developmental conditions is allocated.

title: "Beyond the Language Barrier: Digital Divides and Environmental Participation in Immigrant Communities"
affiliations: Faculty of Environmental and Urban Change, York University

detail.title: "Beyond the Language Barrier: Digital Divides and Environmental Participation in Immigrant Communities"
detail.abstract: Municipal environmental communication strategies increasingly rely on digital platforms, yet these approaches may systematically exclude immigrant communities who face cultural, linguistic, and technological barriers to accessing environmental information. This study examines communication barriers among first-generation immigrants in the Greater Toronto Area through a cross-sectional survey of 815 participants across four age cohorts, measuring English proficiency, digital literacy, and municipal resource awareness. Results reveal substantial disparities in communication accessibility that intensify dramatically with age. English proficiency declined from 73.4% among participants aged 18-35 to 36.8% among those 65+, while digital literacy barriers compounded these challenges, with only 12.4% of older participants comfortable navigating government websites. Municipal resource awareness showed the steepest decline, falling from 59.8% to 5.6% across age groups. Nearly one-quarter of participants (22.3%) faced all three barrier types simultaneously, with environmental program participation rates of only 8.2% among this group compared to 76.4% among those facing no barriers. Analysis revealed that barriers compound each other's effects rather than simply adding together, with communication factors explaining over one-third of participation differences beyond basic demographics. Despite facing multiple communication barriers, 78.9% of participants expressed strong interest in environmental programs when information was made accessible, creating substantial gaps between environmental interest and actual participation across all program types. These findings demonstrate systematic environmental communication exclusion that we term "digital environmental injustice." The results indicate that addressing communication barriers, rather than assuming lack of environmental concern, represents the key opportunity for improving program effectiveness. Recommendations include maintaining non-digital communication options alongside digital improvements, prioritizing multilingual approaches, and partnering with trusted community organizations to ensure equitable environmental participation.

detail.abstract: Widespread electric vehicle use is a key step to tackling transportation emissions, but adoption has yet to take off beyond high-income communities. A lack of access to public charging stations can be a major barrier to adoption. In this paper, we analyze the distribution and typology of public charging stations found in low-, mid-, and high-income communities across the US. Our results identify a robust neighborhood advantage, where high income in the surrounding area coincides with higher numbers of public stations in lower income block groups. We further show that station types in lower income areas are associated with shorter stops, suggesting they are designed to serve pass-through demand. Future income-based policies for public charging infrastructure should consider how new stations fit local residents' mobility patterns and should use both local and neighborhood income to better target their support toward equal access for all future electric vehicle drivers.

detail.abstract: We leverage multimodal large language models (LLMs) to construct a dataset of 306,070 German patents (1877-1918) from 9,562 archival image scans using our LLM-based pipeline powered by Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite. Our benchmarking exercise provides tentative evidence that multimodal LLMs can create higher quality datasets than our research assistants, while also being more than 795 times faster and 205 times cheaper in constructing the patent dataset from our image corpus. About 20 to 50 patent entries are embedded on each page, arranged in a double-column format and printed in Gothic and Roman fonts. The font and layout complexity of our primary source material suggests to us that multimodal LLMs are a paradigm shift in how datasets are constructed in economic history. We open-source our benchmarking and patent datasets as well as our LLM-based data pipeline, which can be easily adapted to other image corpora using LLM-assisted coding tools, lowering the barriers for less technical researchers. Finally, we explain the economics of deploying LLMs for historical dataset construction and conclude by speculating on the potential implications for the field of economic history.

title: The Stagnation Paradox: A Longitudinal Analysis of Structural Limitations in Canadian Extended Producer Responsibility Programs
affiliations: Faculty of Environmental and Urban Change, York University

detail.title: The Stagnation Paradox: A Longitudinal Analysis of Structural Limitations in Canadian Extended Producer Responsibility Programs
detail.abstract:
Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) has emerged as a dominant policy instrument intended to internalize environmental externalities and drive the transition toward a circular economy. However, a longitudinal analysis of Canada's primary EPR jurisdictions—British Columbia, Ontario, Manitoba, and Quebec—reveals a systemic divergence between theoretical promise and empirical reality, characterized as a "stagnation paradox". Utilizing primary financial and operational data from annual stewardship reports, this study documents a trajectory of "escalating costs" and "stagnant returns" within mature recycling systems.

Key empirical findings demonstrate that exponential increases in financial inputs have failed to generate proportionate environmental improvements. In British Columbia, program costs surged by 250% between 2014 and 2023, yet the material recovery rate remained statistically flat. Similarly, Ontario's net system costs nearly tripled over an eighteen-year period, while recovery rates regressed to 53.3%, a figure virtually identical to the baseline recorded nearly two decades prior. The analysis identifies the "evolving tonne"—the shift toward lightweight, complex, and multi-laminate plastics—as a critical structural barrier that renders mechanical recycling infrastructure increasingly inefficient.

Furthermore, the study challenges the economic assumptions of EPR, presenting evidence that compliance costs are passed through to consumers rather than absorbed by producers, thereby functioning as a regressive tax on households. Ultimately, the data suggests that without addressing the disconnect between packaging innovation and waste management infrastructure, EPR risks functioning solely as a mechanism for cost redistribution rather than a driver of environmental performance.

title: Regularized Wishart Stochastic Volatility for High-Dimensional Covariance Forecasting
affiliations: University of Cologne, Department of Economics, Universidade Federal de Santa Catarina (UFSC) and University of Cologne, Germany

detail.title: Regularized Wishart Stochastic Volatility for High-Dimensional Covariance Forecasting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors report there are no competing interests to declare.

detail.abstract: We extend Uhlig's (1994, 1997)Wishart stochastic volatility (WSV) model by introducing a regularized state transition for the precision matrix that shrinks the covariance forecasts toward a  prior reference matrix. This regularization ensures stationarity of the return process and stabilizes the eigenvalues of the covariance forecasts, while preserving closed-form expressions for filtering, prediction, and likelihood evaluation. We provide conditions for stationarity and for the existence of second- and fourth-order moments, show that the model admits a multivariate GARCH representation, and derive bounds that illustrate how regularization prevents degeneracy and excessive dispersion in the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix forecasts. To account for regime shifts in the correlation structure, we further embed a time-varying directional forgetting scheme into the regularized model, allowing the forgetting rate to differ over time and across directions in the return space. In a high-dimensional application with up to 1,000 assets, the regularized models deliver significantly more accurate covariance forecasts than the baseline WSV and perform well compared to several benchmark models.

detail.abstract: Rare genetic diseases collectively affect millions worldwide, yet most remain without effective treatments due to the diversity and complexity of causative mutations. The advent of CRISPR-based in vivo gene editing has ushered in a new era of therapeutic potential, enabling direct correction of disease-causing genetic variants within patient tissues. This paper reviews recent advances in CRISPR delivery systems, therapeutic strategies, clinical successes, ethical considerations, and challenges in translating in vivo gene editing into safe and accessible therapies for rare and previously untreatable diseases. We highlight preclinical and clinical examples, discuss safety and efficacy concerns, and propose future directions for the field.

detail.title: Geometric Analysis of Implied Volatility in Options

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes an internal decomposition of implied volatility, introducing a geometric and economically interpretable framework to analyze the structure and dynamics of the volatility skew. The implied volatility surface is modeled as a continuous equilibrium system, whose shape reflects the interaction of market forces across strikes and maturities.

We introduce the K-EVA framework (Kinetic Equilibrium Volatility Adjustment), which unifies the local volatility approach of Dupire (1994) and the SVI/eSSVI parametrizations (Gatheral, 2004–2016) within a single, arbitrage-consistent representation. Unlike standard approaches focused on functional fitting, K-EVA explicitly decomposes the surface into structural components governing curvature, displacement, level, and asymmetry.

The resulting parameters are stable, dimensionless, and comparable across assets and market regimes. Empirical evidence from liquid Brazilian equity options shows that the proposed decomposition delivers greater geometric consistency and robustness than conventional parametrizations, particularly during stress periods. The framework provides practical tools for mark-to-market, risk diagnostics, and volatility-based hedging strategies.

title: Import-Export Trends of Bangladesh and Their Impact on GDP Growth (1972-2024)

detail.abstract: Examining the trends in imports, exports, and GDP growth in Bangladesh from 1972 to 2024, spanning from post-independence recovery to recent global challenges. Utilizing annual timeseries data from the World Bank World Development Indicators, Bangladesh Bank, and Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics, the study applies descriptive statistics, trend analysis, correlation, and simple linear regression to assess relationships. Findings indicate weak positive correlations between export growth and GDP growth (r = 0.12) and import growth and GDP growth (r = 0.10), with an export-import correlation of 0.36. The regression model (GDP growth = 4.45 + 0.016 Export growth + 0.009 Import growth, R² = 0.019) is insignificant (p = 0.625), suggesting trade growth has a limited direct impact on GDP over the full period, though post-1990 trends show stronger links due to RMG sector expansion. Average GDP growth was 4.65%, exports 9.57%, and imports 6.27%, with volatility in early years and recent slowdowns (e.g., 2020 pandemic). The trade-to-GDP ratio rose from around 13% in the 1970s to 33% in the 2020s, reflecting increased openness but persistent deficits. The economy's susceptibility to shocks underscores the need for export diversification, import management, and complementary policies like remittance and FDI enhancement. This analysis addresses gaps in long-term studies, emphasizing nuanced trade-GDP dynamics beyond export-led growth narratives.

detail.abstract: Georgia is frequently characterized as a business-friendly jurisdiction due to the procedural simplicity of company registration and comparatively liberal economic regulation. However, the true stability of a business environment is determined not by entry formalities, but by the quality and coherence of its dispute resolution mechanisms. This paper examines the system of commercial dispute management in Georgia, focusing on judicial proceedings, arbitration, mediation, corporate reorganization, and insolvency. The analysis demonstrates that these mechanisms serve distinct legal functions and should be understood as components of a broader dispute management architecture rather than as interchangeable remedies. By situating Georgian business law within a comparative and functional framework, the article highlights the structural factors that contribute to its practical attractiveness in a transitional legal system.

title: From Individual Responsibility to Organizational Environment Optimization: A Paradigmatic Transition Toward Post-Neoliberal Organizational Theory

detail.title: From Individual Responsibility to Organizational Environment Optimization: A Paradigmatic Transition Toward Post-Neoliberal Organizational Theory

detail.abstract: This foundational paper introduces the core concepts that inform a broader program of theoretical development in organizational science. Drawing on years of applied experience and preliminary literature review, we propose a paradigmatic transition from approaches centered on individual responsibility toward systematic optimization of organizational environments. We introduce the HOWAR© Formula C = f(I,A) as a new conceptual foundation, establishing the basis for understanding organizational behavior through the dynamic interaction between individual Identity (I) and organizational Ambient environment (A). The paper presents the critical distinction between organizational climate (subjective perceptions) and organizational environment (objective, designable characteristics), along with a five-dimensional environmental framework. This contribution positions environmental quality as the primary lever for sustainable organizational performance while respecting human dignity, laying the groundwork for more comprehensive theoretical elaboration in subsequent work.

title: Naor Revisited: Two-Sided Queues with Strategic Agents
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, Carnegie Mellon University, David A. Tepper School of Business, University of Michigan at Ann Arbor,  and University of Michigan at Ann Arbor - Department of Industrial and Operations Engineering

detail.title: Naor Revisited: Two-Sided Queues with Strategic Agents
detail.abstract: We study a two-sided observable queue where strategic agents arrive on each side according to a Poisson process, seeking to match. Agents decide to join or balk by weighing their matching reward against their expected delay cost until matching. This setting generalizes the seminal one-sided queueing model of Naor (1969) while fundamentally changing the incentive structure: each agent creates both a negative same-side externality and a positive opposite-side externality. We establish the following main results on the equilibrium joining thresholds and performance under self-optimization, social welfare optimization, and profit maximization. (1) These regimes balance the thresholds on both sides in contrasting ways. The self-optimizing thresholds ignore the opposite side's reward and delay cost. The socially optimal thresholds imply that each side's probability of immediate matching is proportional to its delay cost, a newsvendor-like solution. In stark contrast, profit-maximization yields a one-sided queue. (2) Self-optimization may lead to inefficient underjoining, not only on one side, but also in aggregate, yielding lower throughput than socially optimal. However, social optimization may hurt the welfare of one side, compared to self-optimization, pointing to efficiency-equity trade-offs. (3) Social optimization can be implemented via side-specific prices that may require a subsidy on one side, yet guarantee non-negative revenue. (4) The Price of Anarchy (ratio of optimal welfare to self-optimizing welfare) is unbounded and highly sensitive to arrival-rate asymmetries. (5) Profit maximization yields lower throughput than socially optimal, yet the Price of Profit (ratio of optimal welfare to profit-maximizing welfare) is bounded by a factor of 2.

They also successfully create and store health records of patients. They allow patients to check and access their health records anytime with the help of the Internet. These health ATMs have medical devices embedded in them that conduct various tests and research. Method We have design an IoT based smart Health ATMs for Smart Cit. title: The Social Ponzi: A Cognitive Autopsy of the 'Bad Actor'

detail.title: The Social Ponzi: A Cognitive Autopsy of the 'Bad Actor'
detail.abstract: This paper applies a cognitive-behavioral framework to the Zachary Horwitz fraud case, popularly known through the documentary Bad Actor. Rather than treating the fraud as a product of individual pathology or greed, the analysis reframes it as a socially seeded narrative system driven by identity uncertainty, perception management, and Justified Irrational Rationalization (JIRP). The framework generates testable predictions regarding social origin, communicative framing, narrative escalation, and fear hierarchy. Comparison with the public record confirms core predictions while revealing specific informational blind spots-termed Target Variables-that existing accounts do not resolve. The paper demonstrates how cognitive frameworks can function as forensic tools for auditing narrative-driven systems.

title: Indebted Supply and Monetary Policy: A Theory of Financial Dominance
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business, Sciences Po and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Indebted Supply and Monetary Policy: A Theory of Financial Dominance
detail.abstract: We develop a New Keynesian model with financial frictions to study how corporate capital structure shapes static and dynamic monetary policy tradeoffs through the supply side. Ex post, when corporate leverage is high, monetary tightening contracts both demand and supply. As a result, the Phillips curve is highly non-linear and state-dependent, and the "natural rate" Rn ensuring price stability increases with corporate leverage. Yet the tradeoff between in inflation targeting and tightening supply constraints implies that the optimal ex-post policy is to set a rate Ropt < Rn that can decrease with leverage. Ex ante, firms' market-timing incentives lead them to increase leverage when rates are low, which creates an intertemporal tradeoff: monetary easing supports current demand but hurts future supply, which makes easing partially self-defeating. The optimal ex-ante monetary policy features a prudential motive for leaning against leverage even when the divine coincidence holds in the current period.

title: Methodological Variation in Empirical Asset Pricing
affiliations: Saarland University, University of Reading - ICMA Centre and Leibniz  Universität Hannover - Faculty of Economics and Management

detail.title: Methodological Variation in Empirical Asset Pricing
detail.abstract: Empirical asset pricing research exhibits substantial methodological heterogeneity. Analyzing 386 published studies, we document that researchers face over 51,840 unique design-choice combinations in data handling, portfolio sorting, and regression analysis. Key methodological choices vary substantially across studies and are often incompletely documented, complicating replication and comparison. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that methodological choices are systematically associated with reported t-statistics, with data source selection and winsorization of independent variables exhibiting the largest effects. Our results underscore the need for complete methodological disclosure, systematic robustness testing, and standardized reporting to enhance credibility and facilitate cumulative knowledge building in empirical asset pricing.

title: Islam, Politics, and Women in the Public Sphere: Between Institutions, Movements, and Practices
affiliations: Institute for Advanced Study in Toulouse (IAST), Toulouse School of Economics

detail.title: Islam, Politics, and Women in the Public Sphere: Between Institutions, Movements, and Practices
detail.abstract: Bridging interpretive and quantitative research approaches, this chapter synthesizes interdisciplinary discussions of three interrelated inquiries. First, how have major political turning points recast debates about Islam and women’s public roles? Second, how does Islam shape women’s prospects for public participation, whether through state laws and reforms, Islamist parties and movements, or religious practices and interpretations? Third, what does the recent turn to quantitative methods in the study of Islam add to longer-standing debates, and how might it be put into dialogue with qualitative and interpretive approaches?

title: Endogenous Formation of Production Networks with Imperfect Information
affiliations: Université Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne, Climate Finance Alpha

detail.title: Endogenous Formation of Production Networks with Imperfect Information
detail.abstract: We provide a model of the formation of production networks with imperfect information. We consider firms that sequentially explore their local network in search of productivity enhancing technologies. We show that this exploration process generates a Markov process over production networks that converges to equilibrium networks whose structure is determined by the search radius of firms, which we use as a measure of innovativeness. In this setting, we investigate how the structure of equilibrium networks vary with information diffusion and, conversely, how the structure of production networks influence the diffusion of innovations. On the one hand, our model predicts that with increasing information diffusion, production networks become more connected and that their degree distribution shifts to the right. On the second hand, our model provides micro-foundations for the analysis of innovation diffusion as a percolation process. We provide a characterisation of a percolation threshold in terms of the spectral radius, show that technological adoption rates will be suboptimal in general, and that the capacity of an economy to adopt innovations decreases with the percolation threshold. Overall, our model replicates a number of stylized facts of the empirical literature on the diffusion of innovation and provides new testable implications linking the topology of production networks with innovativeness.

title: Triangular Pure Parity Deviations
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business, Johannes Kepler University Linz - Department of Economics and BI Norwegian Business School

detail.title: Triangular Pure Parity Deviations
detail.abstract: We develop a triangular arbitrage methodology to decompose cross-currency basis spreads into two distinct components: currency-specific term funding premium differentials and bilateral pure parity deviations. Using data from seven major currencies spanning 2002-2024, we find that pure parity deviations, which are genuine violations of triangular no-arbitrage, remain economically minimal (under 5 basis points) even during crisis periods, suggesting that international cross-currency markets maintain high efficiency. Term funding premium differentials account for 97-99% of observed bases, reflecting the compensation required for bearing term funding risk across different currencies. We validate this interpretation using cross-currency bond bases constructed from matched-issuer bonds, finding that bond bases net of pure parity closely track swap term funding premium differentials. Since bond yields necessarily embed term funding premia, this convergence confirms our identification. Our results indicate that apparent CIP violations primarily reflect domestic funding market conditions rather than international arbitrage failures. Only the 2022 SOFR transition temporarily disrupted this pattern, creating meaningful pure parity deviations in swap markets that quickly reverted. Our decomposition provides a diagnostic tool distinguishing between domestic funding constraints and bilateral frictions, with distinct policy implications for each component.

title: Do Minorities Pay More to Avoid Flood Risk?

detail.title: Do Minorities Pay More to Avoid Flood Risk?
detail.abstract: Black and Hispanic homebuyers pay 3% more than white buyers for equivalent housing outside flood zones but only 1% more inside flood zones. Using 26M repeatsales transactions (2000-2020) and plausibly exogenous flood zone changes, I show that racial price differentials vary systematically with flood risk. Where flood risk is most salient, premiums for safe housing reach 5% for minority buyers. In highrisk counties, Black and Hispanic buyers pay double the premium white buyers pay for safe housing. As climate change expands flood zones, access to safe housing for minorities may be further restricted, reinforcing inequality and environmental injustice.

title: Public Good or Public Bad? Nation-building and Indigenous Institutions
affiliations: Queen's University Belfast, University of Cologne, Instituto Tecnologico y de Estudios Superiores de Monterrey (ITESM) and Cardiff University

detail.title: Public Good or Public Bad? Nation-building and Indigenous Institutions
detail.abstract: While existing evidence shows that nation-building policies unify societies, little is known about how and what makes some societal groups to resist them. We examine this in the context of the post-Mexican Revolution (1920s-1950s), when the new state implemented a nation-building policy to eliminate Indigenous cultures and identities by increasing connectivity via transport infrastructure. In a difference-in-differences design, we leverage heterogeneity in the exposure to pre-colonial political centralisation as a proxy for the ability of Indigenous populations in mobilising to resist national integration. We find that the expansion of transport infrastructure was lower in municipalities with a stronger efficacy of Indigenous mobilisation. We demonstrate that this underprovision of public goods can be partly explained by Indigenous identity preservation and high abilities for collective actions.

title: Sharpe Proportionality in S&P 500 Buy-Write Strategies: A One-Month Rolling Analysis

detail.title: Sharpe Proportionality in S&P 500 Buy-Write Strategies: A One-Month Rolling Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper provides empirical evidence that the Sharpe ratio of an S&P 500-based Buy-Write strategy exhibits a stable proportional relationship with the Sharpe ratio of its underlying equity index. Extending prior work based on twelve-month rolling windows, this study conducts a onemonth rolling analysis using daily data from January 2008 to December 2025. We find that Buy-Write Sharpe ratios scale linearly with the Sharpe ratios of the underlying index through the origin, with a high degree of explanatory power. When market conditions are classified by excess return and volatility regimes, the proportionality coefficient adjusts systematically across regimes, while the proportional structure itself remains intact. These findings indicate that Sharpe Proportionality is not a long-horizon averaging artifact but a structural feature observable at short time scales. The results are interpreted as empirical evidence for the Risk-Proportionality Principle (RPP), suggesting that Sharpe ratios function as a fundamental unit of risk-adjusted performance transmission in option-based strategies.

title: Submission: Select Committee on the Operation of the Capital Gains Tax Discount

detail.title: Submission: Select Committee on the Operation of the Capital Gains Tax Discount

detail.title: How Computational Complexity can Restore General Equilibrium in Markets with Indivisible Goods
detail.abstract: We study market equilibrium in settings with indivisible goods and tight budget constraints, where a traditional Walrasian Equilibrium (WE) may fail to exist. We introduce the Complexity Compensating Equilibrium (CCE), in which prices endogenously render the budget problem computationally difficult. Complexity induces heterogeneous demands even among agents with homogeneous preferences, as individuals allocate varying levels of cognitive effort. We define the equilibrium region as the set of price configurations that satisfy the necessary economic and computational conditions for equilibrium to exist. In this region, price configurations maximize the difficulty of the budget problem in addition to satisfying market clearing conditions. We evaluate the predictions of CCE through a controlled market experiment. We find that trading prices consistently force the budget problem to the equilibrium region. Further supporting and central to the CCE framework, the equilibrium bundles of goods generate markedly different utility levels across agents. This outcome contradicts a core feature of WE, namely, the equalization of utilities. In a setting where it exists, we reject WE on both prices and utilities, in favor of CCE.

detail.abstract: Effective government budget implementation is crucial to accelerating economic growth in any nation. This study examined the impact of government budget implementation on Nigeria's economic growth from 1981 and 2023 using the neoclassical growth theory. After controlling for inflation (INF) and exchange rates (EXR), it looked at the effects of public debt servicing (PDS), capital expenditure (CAPEX), and recurrent spending (REX) on GDP growth. An autoregressive (AR) model, diagnostic tests, SWOT and PESTEL analyses, time series data from the Central Bank of Nigeria Statistical Bulletin, and World Bank indicators were all used in the study. According to the results, CAPEX (p = 0.979), REX (p = 0.915), and PDS (p = 0.940) were not statistically significant on their own, while the AR (1) term was highly significant (p = 0.002). 37% of the variation in GDP growth was explained by the entire model, which was significant at the 1% level (F-statistic p = 0.009). Economic, institutional, and technological issues impacting budget implementation were further highlighted using SWOT and PESTEL analyses. To promote sustainable economic growth, the study recommends giving priority to profitable capital projects, streamlining ongoing spending, reorganizing debt obligations, and improving budget transparency and participatory monitoring.

detail.title: The Green Inflation Hump: Synthesizing Greenflation, Fossilflation, and Deflationary Dividends in a Non-linear Green Transition Model
detail.abstract: Current ecological macroeconomic literature on the inflationary effect of climate change and the green transition is often polarized between narratives of "Fossilflation" (driven by carbon pricing) and "Greenflation" (driven by mineral and supply chain bottlenecks). This paper argues that standard linear models fail to integrate these dynamics, treating them as conflicting outcomes rather than sequential phases. We propose a methodological synthesis using a dynamic simulation of the Eurozone transition. By modeling green investments as an exponential forcing function against systemic rigidities (𝜒 =22), we identify a "Green Inflation Hump", a non-linear price trajectory with a short to medium term increase and a medium to long-term decrease in overall inflation. Simulating four pathways, we demonstrate a critical policy paradox: attempting to avoid the transition friction of "Greenflation" (via Stagnation) traps the economy in a high-inflation spiral of "Fossilflation," reaching 5.4% by 2040. In contrast, even a "Crash Program" generates a manageable inflation spike (peaking at 2.97%) before delivering deep structural price stability (1.2%).

detail.abstract: This study examines whether U.S. sanctions significantly impact the financing constraints of Chinese listed firms. Using a uniquely constructed dataset of Chinese A-share firms spanning the 2007 to 2021 period that were directly impacted by the U.S. sanctions, we provide strong evidence showing a positive relationship between sanctions and financing constraints. Additional analyses indicate that the positive relationship between sanctions and financing constraints is more (less) pronounced for firms with greater risk exposure (strong market position, strong innovation and research capabilities, and effective government support policies). Sanctions also increase the financing costs for affected firms, shorten their financing duration, and complicate their access to financing. Finally, various endogeneity tests and robustness checks confirm our baseline results. Overall, our study provides important insights into the detrimental effect of U.S. sanctions on Chinese firms' financing constraints.

detail.abstract: Earnings calls serve as a critical platform through which executives communicate firm outlook to the investment community, yet research has only begun to unpack how different top leaders shape market reactions through their language. This study examines how sentiment and linguistic ambiguity expressed by CEOs and CFOs during the question-and-answer (Q&A) portion of earnings calls influence cumulative abnormal returns (CARs). Using a large, multi-year sample of executive responses and a machine-learning–based sentiment framework, we distinguish the informational value of sentiment provided by each role and assess whether ambiguous or imprecise language alters its market impact. The results show that both CEO and CFO sentiment significantly predict CARs, although CEO sentiment exhibits consistently stronger effects. Ambiguity attenuates the informativeness of CFO sentiment but has little moderating influence on CEO sentiment, suggesting that investors perceive vague language as more problematic when used by executives associated with financial accuracy and precision. Marginal-effects analyses further indicate that the influence of sentiment remains robust across varying levels of ambiguity, though the dampening effect for CFOs becomes more pronounced at higher ambiguity levels. These findings underscore the differentiated communicative roles of CEOs and CFOs, illuminate boundary conditions under which sentiment shapes market reactions, and provide new insight into how linguistic cues convey information beyond numerical disclosure.

detail.abstract: Cryptocurrency markets increasingly feature autonomous Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) systems that discover trading strategies through environmental interaction rather than explicit programming. This transition from deterministic High-Frequency Trading (HFT) to adaptive MARL represents a fundamental shift in market microstructure, with profound implications for financial stability and regulatory governance. We demonstrate that when MARL agents operate in partially observable stochastic games with human traders exhibiting loss aversion (Lambda ≈ 2.25), they converge to a stable equilibrium characterized by systematic exploitation of both structural vulnerabilities (mempool transparency, MEV extraction) and behavioral biases (information cascades, panic selling). We formalize this state as the Algorithmic Predatory Equilibrium (APE), prove its Nash equilibrium properties, and establish that current intent-based regulatory frameworks fail to address emergent manipulation strategies that arise autonomously through the learning process. We conclude that traditional enforcement mechanisms are insufficient, necessitating a fundamental shift toward incentive-compatible mechanism design at the protocol level. Our analysis bridges computer science, behavioral finance, and regulatory economics to provide a comprehensive model of AI-driven market manipulation in decentralized finance.

detail.abstract: Expat partners face a distinctive form of career disruption following international relocation, often characterized by identity loss, professional discontinuity, and prolonged uncertainty in host-country labor markets. While existing research has extensively documented structural and institutional barriers to career re-entry, less attention has been paid to the internal psychological resources that enable expat partners to navigate these challenges successfully. This paper examines the role of Psychological Capital (PsyCap)-comprising self-efficacy, hope, optimism, and resilience-as a core mechanism shaping adaptive agency and career reinvention among expat partners. Drawing on theories from positive organizational psychology, career transitions, and migration studies, the article argues that PsyCap functions as a critical protective and enabling factor that supports identity reconstruction, proactive career behaviors, and long-term professional integration. The paper proposes a conceptual framework positioning PsyCap as a mediating resource between relocation-induced disruption and successful career outcomes. The findings offer important implications for global mobility management, HR support programs, and public integration policies, suggesting that the development of Psychological Capital among expat partners is essential for both individual well-being and the overall success of international assignments.

detail.abstract:
METEORAITE presents a systemic synthesis of human evolution within the new cognitive environment reshaped by Artificial Intelligence. This work integrates the concepts of False Cognitive Power Transfer (FCPT) and Minimum Ethical Governance (MEG) – previously published by the author – into a unified theoretical framework dedicated to the "Cognitive Divergence Theory" corpus.
The author proposes a paradigm shift, treating AI not as a tool, but as an "ecological factor" – an unstoppable force with massive disruptive potential that restructures the very architecture of the environment in which human intelligence operates. Much like a meteorite, AI does not seek permission to alter the habitat; it forces immediate biological and social adaptation.
The book traces a long-term evolutionary arc, exploring key moments in the externalization of human power: from the first delegation (Fire), to territorial anchoring (Agriculture), the externalization of memory (Writing), and finally, the externalization of reasoning (AI). The central thesis argues that we are not witnessing mere technological acceleration, but a regime change that the human mind, adapted to gradual variations, is structurally limited to perceive.
By analyzing the stratification mechanisms between "Architects" (L3), "Operators" (L2), and "Passengers" (L1), the book provides a survival manual for cognitive dignity. It is a work of systemic realism where meaning matters more than speed, and lucidity more than enthusiasm.

title: A Universal Law of Computational Allocation in Cognitive Systems
affiliations: Woxsen University

detail.title: A Universal Law of Computational Allocation in Cognitive Systems
detail.abstract: The allocation of computational resources between internal (neural/local) and external (environmental/distributed) systems represents a fundamental constraint on all cognitive architectures. Here we present a universal law governing this allocation: E[C_total] = C_internal + C_external-λ(C_external)•t + ε, where λ represents the atrophy rate as a function of external dependence and t is time. This law, derived from first principles using free energy minimization and information theory, predicts critical phase transitions between sustainable augmentation and irreversible dependency. We validate this law across nine orders of temporal magnitude-from synaptic plasticity (months) to evolutionary regression (millennia)-and demonstrate its applicability to biological neurons, social insect colonies, and artificial intelligence systems. The law predicts that cognitive systems maintaining external support above 65% of total computation for more than 18 months risk irreversible atrophy. With humanity rapidly outsourcing cognitive functions to AI, these findings have immediate implications for education, technology design, and the future of human cognition. We identify emerging "Cognitive Dependency Syndrome" as a new clinical condition and propose quantitative guidelines for sustainable human-AI integration.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence now directly shapes clinical documentation, decision support, and administrative workflows across healthcare. Yet as AI-assisted outputs increasingly influence diagnoses, orders, and reimbursement, healthcare systems lack a foundational governance mechanism to determine who was authorized to invoke AI, under which clinical credentials, and how accountability persists over time. Current approaches emphasize model performance, human review, or post-hoc logging, but fail to establish durable authorship and auditability at the moment AI acts within the clinical workflow. This paper argues that healthcare has reached an inflection point where AI governance must move upstream-from retrospective oversight to credential-governed invocation and immutable provenance of AI-assisted clinical outputs. Drawing on bedside clinical experience and converging regulatory, payer, and liability expectations, it demonstrates why prevailing "human-in-the-loop" frameworks collapse under audit, reimbursement, and litigation scrutiny. A governance architecture is introduced that binds AI invocation and symbolic authorship to verified clinical credentials, producing cryptographically verifiable provenance without disrupting clinical usability. As regulators, payers, and malpractice carriers increasingly demand auditable accountability for AI-mediated actions, credentialgoverned AI authorship is no longer optional. It is becoming prerequisite infrastructure for trusted clinical AI at scale.In prior work, the author examined emerging accountability and governance gaps in AI-assisted clinical workflows (Bryan, SSRN 5241409). This paper advances that analysis by introducing a concrete, upstream governance primitive: credential-governed AI invocation with durable, cryptographically verifiable provenance.

title: The Probability Landscape: A Theory of Orchestrated Intelligence and a Critique of the LLM as a Timeless Reasoner

detail.title: The Probability Landscape: A Theory of Orchestrated Intelligence and a Critique of the LLM as a Timeless Reasoner
detail.abstract:
A fundamental misunderstanding has bifurcated the global debate over Artificial Intelligence. On one side, the "Reasoning Thesis" claims that frontier language models will soon replicate expert judgment at negligible cost. Rich Sutton's "Bitter Lesson," Sam Altman's predictions of near-zero marginal cost intelligence, Vinod Khosla's forecast that 80% of medical work will be automated, and Matt Welsh's proclamation of "The End of Programming" all share this conviction. On the other side, critics like Yann LeCun counter that LLMs are merely "statistical autocomplete," arguing that statistical prediction is fundamentally incapable of genuine cognition. Against the 95% enterprise AI failure rate documented by MIT's Project NANDA, this paper argues that both positions fundamentally misunderstand what determines model output.

The probability distribution over tokens is conditioned on input. Encode meta-cognitive classification, adversarial self-testing, and assumption verification into the input space, and the mechanism remains statistical while the output becomes functionally indistinguishable from the higher-order cognition critics claim is impossible. The misunderstanding is structural: AI development has proceeded without the disciplines that study how language communicates, how knowledge transfers, and how expertise develops. Linguistics, cognitive science, and philosophy of language have been systematically excluded from the rooms where architectural decisions are made.

This insight dissolves the autocomplete objection while revealing what the Reasoning Thesis overlooks: the orchestration that induces higher-order outputs requires human expertise in domain knowledge, communication context, and tacit judgment. This paper demonstrates three structural barriers that retrieval cannot overcome: the Communication Gap, where user intent operates at levels literal prompts cannot capture; the Tacit Barrier, where critical knowledge resists articulation; and the Developmental Barrier, where expertise emerges through irreducible trajectories that cannot be compressed or transmitted.

The paper introduces the Knowledge Delta to name this persistent gap between AI capability and expert judgment, a gap that relocates rather than closes. When AI commoditizes one layer of expertise, value shifts to the next layer. The horizon recedes as capabilities advance. The expert who once produced now validates. The expert who once executed now orchestrates. Human expertise has been relocated rather than rendered obsolete.

Against this gap, operational methodologies are presented from a four-year case study in real estate appraisal: the Delta Index architecture for encoding expert judgment into retrieval systems, Metacognitive Alignment for validating that encoded instructions function under retrieval conditions, and the VOICE Protocol addressing the incentive gap that currently discourages domain experts from contributing their knowledge to AI systems. These methodologies rest on technical architectures whose full specifications invite collaboration between cognitive science and engineering communities for empirical validation.

The moat lies in the judgment to structure the input space such that statistically likely outputs align with expert standards. The soft skills, it turns out, are the hard infrastructure.
